title: Relational Databases (Advanced)
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Explain how the General Purpose, Business Critical and Hyperscale tiers keep a database available inside one region, and what zone redundancy adds.
- Design cross-region disaster recovery with active geo-replication or failover groups, and state the RPO and RTO you can honestly promise.
- Recover from human mistakes with point-in-time restore and long-term retention, and choose a backup storage redundancy.
- Choose the right security, scaling and performance features: Entra-only authentication, TDE with customer-managed keys, Always Encrypted, dynamic data masking, row-level security, auditing, Microsoft Defender for SQL, read scale-out, elastic pools and Query Store.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

Since Lunch 11 the orders have lived in Azure SQL Database. No more USB drive, no more shared sa password. Then Ibu Sari reads a news story about a cloud outage that took a whole region offline for an afternoon, and she brings it to the Monday meeting: "If that happens to our region, how long can't we sell — and how many orders do we lose?"

The rest of the table has requests of its own. The customer service team needs to look up orders but should not see full e-mail addresses and phone numbers. Finance must keep month-end copies of the data for years. And on Friday Dewi ran an UPDATE without a WHERE clause on the test database — "only" the test database, this time.

Today you make the orders survive three different disasters: a failed zone, a failed region and a failed human. You also lock the data down from the inside. How much data could Nusantara Retail lose if a whole Azure region failed, and how quickly could it sell again?

Reading

1. High availability inside one region

Azure SQL Database keeps more than one copy of every database and fails over automatically when hardware, software or the network fails, and during planned maintenance such as patching. You do not configure any of this; your part is retry logic in the application, because a failover shows up as a short disconnect. How the copies are kept depends on the service tier:

- General Purpose (and the DTU tiers Basic and Standard) uses remote storage. The database engine runs on a stateless compute node, while data and log files sit in Azure Storage, which keeps its own copies. If the node fails, the platform starts the engine on a spare node and attaches the same files.
- Business Critical (and Premium) uses local storage. A cluster of database engine replicas — a primary and up to three secondaries — each holds a full copy of the data on fast local SSD. A transaction commits only when a quorum of replicas has it, so a failover is quick and loses nothing. One secondary is readable at no extra cost.
- Hyperscale splits the engine into parts: compute replicas, page servers that each hold a slice of the data, a log service, and long-term storage. You can add zero to four high-availability replicas and up to 30 named replicas, and the database can grow to 128 TB.

Zone redundancy spreads those copies across the region's availability zones (Lunch 03). It is available for General Purpose, Business Critical, Hyperscale and Premium, but not for Basic or Standard. For Hyperscale you must choose it when you create the database. With zone redundancy, a whole zone can fail and the database keeps running after a short failover. Microsoft's business continuity guidance describes this as no data loss and a recovery time typically under 30 seconds.

Tier | Where the data lives | Built-in readable copy | Zone redundancy | Best for
Basic / Standard (DTU) | remote storage | no | no | small, non-critical databases
General Purpose | remote storage | no | yes | most business workloads
Business Critical / Premium | local SSD on several replicas | yes, one secondary | yes | low latency, fast failover, heavy reporting
Hyperscale | page servers + log service + Azure Storage | yes, with HA or named replicas | yes, chosen at creation | large or fast-growing databases

What does a failover look like from the application's side? Open connections drop, and for a few seconds new ones may fail with a transient error such as 40613, "database not currently available". An app that waits briefly and tries again — with growing pauses between attempts — never notices. An app without retry logic shows customers an error page for every failover and every patch. Most modern data-access libraries include a retry option; turning it on is one of the cheapest reliability improvements you can make.

High availability answers "what if a server or a zone fails?". It does not answer Ibu Sari's question, because all of these copies live in one region.

2. Disaster recovery across regions: geo-replication and failover groups

To survive a regional outage you need a copy of the data in another region. Azure SQL Database offers three ways.

Geo-restore is the budget option. If your backups use geo-redundant storage, you can restore the latest replicated backup into any region. Nothing runs in the second region until you need it, but you lose the changes made since that backup was replicated, and the restore itself takes time that grows with the database size. Plan for minutes to hours.

Active geo-replication works per database. You create up to four readable geo-secondaries, usually in other regions. The primary sends its transaction log to them asynchronously: a transaction commits on the primary first and travels to the secondaries a moment later. Failover is manual and per database. After a failover the new primary has a different server name, so every connection string must change.

Failover groups build on geo-replication and fix that connection-string problem. A failover group replicates some or all databases of one logical server to a server in another region, and fails them over together. Generally available failover groups have one secondary server; more secondaries were in preview at the time of writing. Each group gets two listener names that never change:

- <fog-name>.database.windows.net — the read-write listener, always pointing at the current primary;
- <fog-name>.secondary.database.windows.net — the read-only listener, pointing at the secondary.

The listeners are DNS aliases with a 30-second time-to-live. After a failover, the names stay the same and their targets swap, so applications reconnect without any configuration change — provided they retry.

Failovers come in two kinds. A planned failover first synchronises the secondary fully, then swaps the roles, so it loses nothing; use it for drills and for moving between regions. A forced failover (--allow-data-loss) swaps immediately, so transactions committed on the primary but not yet shipped are lost. You also choose a failover policy. Customer managed (recommended by Microsoft) means you decide when to fail over. Microsoft managed means Microsoft fails over all such groups in a region during a widespread outage, and only after a grace period of at least one hour.

Now Ibu Sari's numbers. The RPO (how much data you can lose) of asynchronous replication equals the replication lag: the changes the secondary has not received yet. It is usually seconds. You can watch it in the replication_lag_sec column of sys.dm_geo_replication_link_status on the primary. The RTO (how long you are down) is your decision time plus the failover itself; Microsoft's guidance quotes typically less than 60 seconds once a customer-managed failover starts.

| Geo-restore | Active geo-replication | Failover group
Scope | one database | one database | a group of databases
Secondary running all the time | no | yes, up to four, readable | yes, one secondary server (GA)
Connection after failover | new database name | new server name | same listener names
Typical RPO | since the last replicated backup | replication lag (seconds) | replication lag (seconds)
Typical RTO | minutes to hours | under a minute once started | under a minute once started
Extra cost | none until used | secondary compute and storage | secondary compute and storage

Two design choices deserve care. When you create a failover group, the secondary is first seeded with a full copy of each database, which takes longer for large databases. And the secondary should have the same service tier and compute size as the primary. A smaller secondary falls behind under a heavy write load, which raises your RPO, and it becomes the bottleneck the moment it turns into the primary. If the secondary exists purely for disaster recovery, vCore General Purpose and Business Critical databases can use a licence-free standby secondary to reduce cost.

Tip: Rehearse before you need it. A failover drill is a planned failover during a quiet hour: announce it, fail over, check that the app reconnects through the listener and that reports still run, write down how long each step took, then fail back the same way. A team that has done this twice will make the real decision in minutes, not hours.

Warning: A failover group copies databases, not the server around them. Server-level firewall rules, the server's Entra admin and server-level auditing must be configured on the secondary server too, or the first failover becomes a second outage. Database-level items — contained users, database-level firewall rules, masking rules — travel with the database.

Region pairs (Lunch 03) do not limit you: geo-replication works between any two regions. That matters for Indonesia Central, which has no paired region. If customer data must stay in Indonesia, check with your compliance team before you place a replica abroad.

3. Backups in depth: the undo button

Replication is not a backup. Dewi's UPDATE without a WHERE clause reaches every geo-secondary within seconds, faithfully copied. To undo a mistake, you go back in time with backups.

Azure SQL Database takes full backups weekly, differential backups every 12 or 24 hours, and log backups about every 10 minutes. Point-in-time restore (PITR) rebuilds the database as it was at any moment in the retention window — 7 days by default, configurable from 1 to 35 days (Basic: up to 7) — into a new database on the same server. You compare, copy the rows you need back, or switch the application over. Three details trip people up. First, a new database has no restore points yet: the first full backup starts right after creation and usually finishes within 30 minutes, and PITR becomes possible after the first log backup that follows it. Second, you cannot run PITR on a geo-secondary; restore from the primary. Third, a deleted database can also be restored while it is inside its retention window.

Take Dewi's mistake as a worked example. She ran the bad UPDATE at 16:59. You restore the database as it was at 16:58 into sqldb-orders-restored and compare the two copies. If only a few rows changed, you copy the correct values back with your usual tools while the shop keeps selling. If the damage is widespread, you point the application at the restored copy instead. Either way, the more precisely you know when the mistake happened, the less good data you throw away — another reason to keep auditing on.

Long-term retention (LTR) keeps selected weekly, monthly and yearly full backups for up to 10 years — the answer to finance's month-end request. Backup storage redundancy decides where the backup files live: locally redundant (LRS), zone-redundant (ZRS), geo-redundant (GRS, the default) or geo-zone-redundant (GZRS). Only GRS and GZRS make geo-restore possible. You can change it later, but only future backups use the new setting (it can take up to 48 hours); the free offer supports LRS only, and not every option exists in every region — check yours.

Problem | First tool to reach for
Someone deleted or changed rows by mistake | point-in-time restore to a new database
Someone dropped the whole database | restore the deleted database
One availability zone fails | zone redundancy (automatic)
The whole region is unavailable | failover group failover (or geo-restore)
An auditor wants month-end data from three years ago | long-term retention backup

4. Scaling and performance

You can change the number of vCores or the service tier while the database stays online; only a short reconnect happens at the end. Serverless compute (Lunch 11) scales automatically. Elastic pools share capacity between many databases whose peaks happen at different times. Hyperscale grows storage on its own and adds compute quickly, because the data does not have to be copied to new nodes.

Reporting is a classic performance problem: one heavy month-end query slows down checkout for everyone. Read scale-out solves it in Premium, Business Critical and Hyperscale, where it is on by default. Add ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly to the reporting tool's connection string and its queries run on a read-only replica at no extra cost. A failover group's read-only listener does the same across regions.

To find out why a query is slow, start with Query Store, which is on by default in Azure SQL Database. It works like a flight recorder, keeping queries, their execution plans and runtime statistics over time, so you can see when a plan changed for the worse. Automatic tuning acts on that data: FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN is on by default and reverts to the previous plan when a new one regresses. CREATE_INDEX and DROP_INDEX can add and remove indexes for you, but they are off by default.

Measure before you scale. The database's metrics show whether CPU, data I/O or log I/O is the bottleneck. If one badly written query is to blame, more vCores only make the problem more expensive; fixing the query or adding the right index is cheaper and lasts longer.

5. Security in layers

Lunch 15 introduced defense in depth. For a database, the layers look like this:

Layer | Feature | Protects against | Does not protect against
Network | firewall rules; private endpoints with public access disabled | connections from unknown networks | a signed-in insider
Identity | Microsoft Entra-only authentication, managed identities, least-privilege roles | stolen or shared passwords | an over-privileged account
Data at rest | TDE with a service-managed or customer-managed key | stolen disks and backup files | anyone allowed to query
Sensitive columns | Always Encrypted | administrators reading plaintext; data stays encrypted in the engine | a compromised client that holds the keys
Query results | dynamic data masking | casual exposure, such as support staff seeing full e-mails | determined users who infer values with clever queries
Rows | row-level security | users seeing other stores' rows | users with broad rights who can change the policy
Detection | auditing; Microsoft Defender for SQL | unnoticed misuse, SQL injection, vulnerable settings | nothing by itself — someone must act on the alerts

A few details matter in practice. Transparent data encryption is on for every new database. With a customer-managed key in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM you control rotation, and revoking the key makes the database inaccessible — so both servers of a failover group need access to it. Always Encrypted encrypts selected columns in the client driver, so the database engine never sees the plaintext; secure enclaves allow richer queries on encrypted columns.

Dynamic data masking is the opposite trade-off: the data is stored in clear text, and only query results are masked for users without the UNMASK permission. The server admin, the Microsoft Entra admin and members of db_owner always see real values. Masking functions include default, email, random, custom string and datetime; for example ALTER TABLE dbo.Customers ALTER COLUMN Email ADD MASKED WITH (FUNCTION = 'email()');. Row-level security uses a predicate function and a security policy to filter rows per user — store managers in Medan see only Medan's orders.

Auditing writes database events to a storage account, a Log Analytics workspace or Event Hubs; Microsoft recommends enabling it at the server level. Microsoft Defender for SQL adds vulnerability assessment and alerts for threats such as SQL injection and unusual sign-ins, as a paid plan.

Security and disaster recovery meet in one more place. With private endpoints, each server in a failover group needs its own endpoint in a virtual network in its own region, and private DNS that resolves the names correctly in both regions. Lunch 25 shows how private DNS zones work; design them for the failover case from the start.

6. PostgreSQL, MySQL and the plan for Nusantara Retail

The open-source engines from Lunch 11 have their own resilience features. Azure Database for PostgreSQL and Azure Database for MySQL flexible servers offer high availability with a standby server in another zone (zone-redundant) or in the same zone, kept in sync synchronously. Failover is automatic and typically takes 60–120 seconds. HA is not available on the Burstable compute tier. For reads and for regional DR, both offer asynchronous read replicas, which you can place in other regions and promote. PostgreSQL allows up to five replicas per server (more with cascading replicas), MySQL up to ten. Azure SQL Managed Instance has no active geo-replication, but it supports failover groups for the whole instance, with the same listener idea.

Back to Nusantara Retail. Here is the plan you take to Ibu Sari:

- Zone failure: the orders database runs on General Purpose with zone redundancy in its home region. A zone outage costs a short reconnect and no data.
- Region failure: a failover group with a customer-managed policy replicates to a second region, after the compliance team approves where the DR copy may live. The storefront connects through the read-write listener; store reports use the read-only listener. The team rehearses a planned failover every quarter.
- Human failure: PITR retention is raised to 14 days, and LTR keeps monthly backups for the period finance requires.
- Inside the database: Entra-only authentication with a managed identity for the app, a private endpoint (Lunch 25), dynamic data masking on customer e-mail and phone for the support team, row-level security for store managers, server-level auditing to Log Analytics (Lunch 30), and Defender for SQL.

The answer to Ibu Sari's question is honest rather than perfect. In a regional disaster, Nusantara Retail could lose the orders still in flight — the replication lag, usually seconds. It can sell again within minutes of the decision to fail over, and the drill tells everyone exactly who makes that decision.

Pause and think: Dewi suggests the Microsoft-managed failover policy "so Azure handles it for us". What would that mean for Nusantara Retail's recovery time during a regional outage, and who would decide when the shop moves to the other region?

Field notes from Stefanus

A failover group is a decision, not a feature. In design reviews I ask two questions about every failover group. First: who decides to fail over at two in the morning, and who is their deputy? With the customer-managed policy, Azure waits for a human, so that human needs a name, a runbook and the authority to act. Second: which connection strings still contain a server name? I search the app settings for database.windows.net; every hit that is not a listener name will break on the first failover. Then I test the undo button the same way: once a quarter, I ask the team to restore yesterday's database to a new name and time it. A backup you have never restored is only a hope.

Go further

- Microsoft Learn: Failover groups overview & best practices (Azure SQL Database) (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-sql/database/failover-group-sql-db) — listeners, failover policies, initial seeding and the permissions you need.
- Microsoft Learn: Availability through redundancy (Azure SQL Database) (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-sql/database/high-availability-sla-local-zone-redundancy) — the remote-storage, local-storage and Hyperscale availability models, with and without zones.
- Microsoft Learn: Automated backups in Azure SQL Database (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-sql/database/automated-backups-overview) — backup frequency, retention and backup storage redundancy in detail.
- Microsoft Learn: Dynamic data masking (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-sql/database/dynamic-data-masking-overview) — masking functions, permissions and limitations.

quiz.q: The orders database is in a failover group, but the storefront's connection string still uses sql-nusa-main-ab12c.database.windows.net. After a failover to the secondary region, checkout fails with "the database is read-only". Why, and what is the fix?
quiz.a: The app still connects to the old primary, which is now the read-only secondary. Use the read-write listener <fog-name>.database.windows.net, whose target follows the primary through every failover.

quiz.q: Twenty minutes ago someone ran DELETE FROM dbo.Orders without a WHERE clause. Will a failover to the secondary region bring the rows back?
quiz.a: No. Replication copied the delete to the secondary within seconds. Run a point-in-time restore of the primary to a moment just before the delete, into a new database, and copy the rows back.

quiz.q: Ibu Sari asks: "With a failover group, can we promise zero data loss if the whole region goes down?" What do you answer?
quiz.a: Not for an unplanned outage. Replication is asynchronous, so a forced failover can lose the transactions not yet replicated — the RPO equals the replication lag, usually seconds. Only planned failovers synchronise first and lose nothing.

quiz.q: Customer service should see orders but not customers' full e-mail addresses, without changing the application. Which feature fits, and who will still see the real values?
quiz.a: Dynamic data masking, for example the email() function on the Email column. Admins, db_owner members and anyone granted UNMASK still see real values. To hide data even from administrators, you would need Always Encrypted instead.

quiz.q: Month-end reports slow down checkout on a Business Critical database. What is the cheapest way to move the reports off the primary?
quiz.a: Read scale-out. Add ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly to the reporting connection string so its queries run on the built-in readable secondary replica, at no extra cost.

takeaways: High availability is built in; zone redundancy (General Purpose, Business Critical, Hyperscale, Premium) lets a database survive a zone outage without data loss.
Failover groups replicate asynchronously to another region and give you listener names that follow the primary; RPO equals the replication lag, and RTO is your decision time plus the failover.
Replication copies mistakes too — point-in-time restore (1–35 days) and long-term retention (up to 10 years) are the undo button, and you cannot run PITR on a geo-secondary.
Secure a database in layers: network (private endpoints), identity (Entra-only), data (TDE, Always Encrypted, masking, row-level security) and detection (auditing, Defender for SQL).
Scale and tune with vCores, elastic pools, Hyperscale, read scale-out, Query Store and automatic tuning; PostgreSQL and MySQL flexible servers offer zone-redundant HA and read replicas.

lab.title: Orders that survive a regional outage
lab.text:
What you'll build

Nusantara Retail's orders database gets a disaster recovery plan. setup.sh gives you two logical servers that accept only Microsoft Entra sign-ins — one in your lab region ($LOCATION) and one in a second region ($SECONDARY_LOCATION) — plus a small sqldb-orders database with customers and orders. You then mask customer contact details for the support team, put the database in a failover group and connect through its listeners. After a deliberate "oops" you recover deleted orders with point-in-time restore, and you finish with a planned failover drill that moves the primary to the second region. Optionally, you send audit logs to Log Analytics.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you can create resources (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)). Sign in with a user account: the lab makes that account the Microsoft Entra admin of both servers.
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. It already has the Azure CLI and sqlcmd.
- Your subscription must be allowed to create SQL servers in two regions. The defaults are southeastasia and its pair eastasia; any two different regions work.
- Get the lab files and load the shared settings and the names you will reuse:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/28-relational-databases-advanced
source ../common/config.sh
RG=$(rg_name 28); RG_DR=$(rg_name 28 dr)
SQL_MAIN="sql-nusa-main-${SUFFIX}"; SQL_DR="sql-nusa-dr-${SUFFIX}"
MAIN_FQDN="${SQL_MAIN}.database.windows.net"
FOG="fog-nusa-${SUFFIX}"
FOG_RW="${FOG}.database.windows.net"; FOG_RO="${FOG}.secondary.database.windows.net"
DB=sqldb-orders
source azsql.sh            # defines 'azsql': sqlcmd with your Microsoft Entra token

- Create the starting point — takes about 10 minutes:

bash setup.sh

Tip: Cloud Shell ends a session after about 20 minutes without activity. If that happens, cd back into the lab folder and run the variable block above again. If Cloud Shell also got a new public IP address, run bash setup.sh once more: it is safe to repeat and refreshes the firewall rules on both servers.

Important: The logical servers are free, but the three small databases you end up with — the primary, its geo-secondary and the restored copy — cost money while they exist (cents per hour). Finish with the Clean up section, even if you stop halfway.

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | run setup.sh, then follow Tasks 1–7 below
Challenge | you already know the basics | read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Task 1 · Inspect the starting point

Before you add disaster recovery, check what you are protecting and where it lives.

az sql server list --query "[?starts_with(name, 'sql-nusa-')].{server:name, region:location, group:resourceGroup}" --output table
az sql db show --resource-group "$RG" --server "$SQL_MAIN" --name "$DB" \
  --query "{tier:currentServiceObjectiveName, backups:currentBackupStorageRedundancy, earliestRestore:earliestRestoreDate}" --output table
azsql "$MAIN_FQDN" "$DB" -W -Q "SELECT StoreCode, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM dbo.Orders GROUP BY StoreCode ORDER BY StoreCode;"

Notice three things. The database uses the Basic tier — the cheapest tier that supports failover groups (the free offer cannot join one). Its backups are locally redundant, which keeps the lab cheap and works in every region; a production plan that relies on geo-restore needs geo-redundant backup storage. And earliestRestore may still be empty: a brand-new database gets its first restore point once the first full backup and the log backup after it complete, usually within about 30 minutes. You will need it in Task 5.

Checkpoint: two servers in two different regions; sqldb-orders is Basic; the query lists nine orders, three of them for SBY-01 (Surabaya).

Task 2 · Mask customer e-mail addresses and phone numbers

The customer service team needs to look up customers, but not to see their full contact details. Dynamic data masking hides values in query results for users without the UNMASK permission; the stored data does not change. Read masking.sql first. It masks Email with the email() function and Phone with a partial() function, and creates a test user, support_agent, without a login.

azsql "$MAIN_FQDN" "$DB" -i masking.sql

Now compare what you see as the admin with what the support team sees. EXECUTE AS USER lets you impersonate the test user inside your own session:

azsql "$MAIN_FQDN" "$DB" -W -Q "SELECT TOP (3) FullName, Email, Phone FROM dbo.Customers ORDER BY CustomerId;"
azsql "$MAIN_FQDN" "$DB" -W -Q "EXECUTE AS USER = 'support_agent'; SELECT TOP (3) FullName, Email, Phone FROM dbo.Customers ORDER BY CustomerId; REVERT;"

You do this before creating the failover group on purpose: masking rules live inside the database, so they will be replicated to the secondary with everything else.

Tip: Prefer the portal? SQL databases › sqldb-orders › Security › Dynamic Data Masking shows the masked columns and lets you add rules — compare it with the result of the script.

Checkpoint: as the admin you see addresses such as andi.pratama@example.com; as support_agent you see masked values such as aXXX@XXXX.com and XXXX-XXXX-XX01. masking.sql listed two masked columns.

Task 3 · Create the failover group

A failover group replicates the database to the server in the second region and gives you two listener names that follow the roles. The name becomes a DNS name, so it must be globally unique; the suffix takes care of that. --failover-policy Manual is the customer-managed policy that Microsoft recommends: you decide when to fail over.

az sql failover-group create \
  --name "$FOG" \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --server "$SQL_MAIN" \
  --partner-server "$SQL_DR" \
  --partner-resource-group "$RG_DR" \
  --failover-policy Manual \
  --add-db "$DB" \
  --output none

Azure now seeds the secondary: it creates sqldb-orders on the DR server and copies the data. For this small database that takes a few minutes. While you wait, re-read section 2 of the lunch.

az sql failover-group show --resource-group "$RG" --server "$SQL_MAIN" --name "$FOG" \
  --query "{group:name, roleOfMainServer:replicationRole, policy:readWriteEndpoint.failoverPolicy}" --output table
az sql db replica list-links --resource-group "$RG" --server "$SQL_MAIN" --name "$DB" \
  --query "[].{partner:partnerServer, partnerRole:partnerRole, state:replicationState}" --output table

Tip: Prefer the portal? SQL servers › sql-nusa-main-… › Data management › Failover groups › + Add group. The map view shows both regions and the replication direction.

Checkpoint: roleOfMainServer is Primary, the policy is Manual, and the replication link to the DR server reaches the CATCH_UP state (that means seeding is finished and changes are flowing).

Task 4 · Connect through the listeners and measure the lag

Applications should never use a server name for a database in a failover group. They use the read-write listener (always the primary) or the read-only listener (the secondary). Ask each one where you actually landed:

azsql "$FOG_RW" "$DB" -W -Q "SELECT @@SERVERNAME AS server_name, DATABASEPROPERTYEX(DB_NAME(), 'Updateability') AS updateability;"
azsql "$FOG_RO" "$DB" -K ReadOnly -W -Q "SELECT @@SERVERNAME AS server_name, DATABASEPROPERTYEX(DB_NAME(), 'Updateability') AS updateability;"

-K ReadOnly declares read-only intent, which is what a reporting tool should do. Now look at the replication link from the primary's point of view. replication_lag_sec is your RPO right now: the seconds of changes that a forced failover would lose.

azsql "$FOG_RW" "$DB" -W -Q "SELECT partner_server, role_desc, replication_state_desc, replication_lag_sec, last_replication FROM sys.dm_geo_replication_link_status;"

Checkpoint: the read-write listener lands on sql-nusa-main-… with READ_WRITE; the read-only listener lands on sql-nusa-dr-… with READ_ONLY. The lag is a small number of seconds, often 0 for an idle database.

Task 5 · Oops! Recover deleted orders with point-in-time restore

First make sure a restore point exists — a brand-new database cannot be restored to a moment before its first backup:

az sql db show --resource-group "$RG" --server "$SQL_MAIN" --name "$DB" --query earliestRestoreDate --output tsv

If this prints nothing, wait five minutes and ask again; meanwhile, read section 3 of the lunch. When it shows a time, note the current time in UTC, then make the mistake on purpose:

BEFORE_OOPS=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S); echo "Restore point: $BEFORE_OOPS UTC"
sleep 5
azsql "$FOG_RW" "$DB" -Q "DELETE FROM dbo.Orders WHERE StoreCode = 'SBY-01';"

Did the failover group protect you? Ask the secondary:

azsql "$FOG_RO" "$DB" -K ReadOnly -W -Q "SELECT COUNT(*) AS sby_orders_on_secondary FROM dbo.Orders WHERE StoreCode = 'SBY-01';"

Zero. Replication copied the mistake within seconds — replication is not a backup. Restore the database as it was just before the delete, into a new database on the main server:

az sql db restore \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --server "$SQL_MAIN" \
  --name "$DB" \
  --dest-name sqldb-orders-restored \
  --time "$BEFORE_OOPS" \
  --service-objective Basic \
  --backup-storage-redundancy Local \
  --output none

A restore usually takes several minutes, even for a tiny database. If the command says the point in time is not valid yet, a log backup is still pending: wait ten minutes and run it again. The restored copy is not part of the failover group, so you reach it through the main server's own name:

azsql "$MAIN_FQDN" sqldb-orders-restored -W -Q "SELECT COUNT(*) AS sby_orders_in_restored_copy FROM dbo.Orders WHERE StoreCode = 'SBY-01';"

Tip: Prefer the portal? SQL databases › sqldb-orders › Restore shows the earliest restore point and lets you pick the time with a date picker.

Checkpoint: the restored copy has three SBY-01 orders while the live database has none. az sql db list --resource-group "$RG" --server "$SQL_MAIN" --query "[].name" --output tsv lists sqldb-orders-restored. (Putting the rows back is a stretch goal.)

Task 6 · Run a planned failover drill

Time to move the primary to the second region without losing anything. set-primary runs against the server that should become the primary. Without --allow-data-loss it is a planned failover: Azure synchronises the secondary fully, then swaps the roles.

az sql failover-group set-primary --name "$FOG" --resource-group "$RG_DR" --server "$SQL_DR"
az sql failover-group show --name "$FOG" --resource-group "$RG_DR" --server "$SQL_DR" \
  --query "{group:name, roleOfDrServer:replicationRole}" --output table

The listener names did not change, but their targets did. DNS caches the old answer for up to 30 seconds, so wait a minute, then connect with exactly the same command as in Task 4 and write a new order:

azsql "$FOG_RW" "$DB" -W -Q "SELECT @@SERVERNAME AS server_name, DATABASEPROPERTYEX(DB_NAME(), 'Updateability') AS updateability;"
azsql "$FOG_RW" "$DB" -Q "INSERT INTO dbo.Orders (CustomerId, StoreCode, TotalIdr) VALUES (4, 'JKT-02', 315000);"

The DR server could take over only because setup.sh gave it the same Entra admin and a firewall rule for your IP address — server-level settings are not replicated.

Checkpoint: roleOfDrServer is Primary; the read-write listener now lands on sql-nusa-dr-… with READ_WRITE, and the insert succeeds.

Task 7 (optional) · Send audit logs to Log Analytics

Auditing records who did what in the database. Microsoft recommends server-level auditing, configured on both servers so that it keeps working after a failover.

az monitor log-analytics workspace create --resource-group "$RG" --workspace-name log-nusa --location "$LOCATION" --output none
LAW_ID=$(az monitor log-analytics workspace show --resource-group "$RG" --workspace-name log-nusa --query id --output tsv)
az sql server audit-policy update --resource-group "$RG" --name "$SQL_MAIN" --state Enabled --lats Enabled --lawri "$LAW_ID" --output none
az sql server audit-policy update --resource-group "$RG_DR" --name "$SQL_DR" --state Enabled --lats Enabled --lawri "$LAW_ID" --output none
az sql server audit-policy show --resource-group "$RG_DR" --name "$SQL_DR" --query "{state:state, toAzureMonitor:isAzureMonitorTargetEnabled}" --output table

Run a couple of queries with azsql, wait 10–15 minutes, then open Log Analytics workspaces › log-nusa › Logs and run:

AzureDiagnostics
| where Category == "SQLSecurityAuditEvents"
| project TimeGenerated, server_principal_name_s, action_name_s, statement_s
| order by TimeGenerated desc
| take 20

Checkpoint: the audit policy shows Enabled; after a few minutes the query returns your own statements, signed with your Entra identity. (If the project line complains about a column, remove it to see every column.)

Break it and fix it

Dewi's old storefront configuration still points at a server name. Play the old app: write to the database through the main server's name instead of the listener.

azsql "$MAIN_FQDN" "$DB" -Q "INSERT INTO dbo.Orders (CustomerId, StoreCode, TotalIdr) VALUES (1, 'JKT-01', 120000);"

Symptom: Msg 3906 … Failed to update database "sqldb-orders" because the database is read-only. The connection works — the old primary is now a readable geo-secondary — but every write fails. In a real outage that server might not answer at all.

Hint: how to fix it

Connect through the read-write listener, whose target follows the primary through every failover:

azsql "$FOG_RW" "$DB" -Q "INSERT INTO dbo.Orders (CustomerId, StoreCode, TotalIdr) VALUES (1, 'JKT-01', 120000);"

In an application, that means Server=tcp:fog-nusa-<suffix>.database.windows.net,1433 in the connection string — plus retry logic, because every failover drops open connections.

Verify your work

bash verify.sh

Every check should say PASS. If one fails, the message tells you which task to revisit. verify.sh expects the DR server to be the primary (Task 6). If you failed back on purpose, run EXPECTED_PRIMARY=main bash verify.sh.

Clean up (do not skip!)

bash cleanup.sh

The script deletes things in the right order: first the failover group, then the geo-replication link (deleting a failover group does not stop replication), then both resource groups rg-lunch28-<suffix> and rg-lunch28-dr-<suffix> with the servers, the databases, the restored copy and the Log Analytics workspace. Deletion continues in the background for a few minutes.

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
Location '…' is not accepting creation of new Windows Azure SQL Database servers for the subscription '…' at this time. | Your subscription cannot create SQL servers in that region | Run bash cleanup.sh and wait until az group list --tag lunch=28 --output table is empty (the resource groups already exist in the old regions), then export SECONDARY_LOCATION=<another region> (or LOCATION), source ../common/config.sh and bash setup.sh
Error 40615: Client with IP address '…' is not allowed to access the server | Cloud Shell has a new public IP, or you connect to a server without a rule for you | Run bash setup.sh again — it refreshes the rule on both servers — then wait up to five minutes
Msg 3906: Failed to update database … because the database is read-only | You are writing to the geo-secondary: a server name or the read-only listener | Write through $FOG_RW; right after a failover, wait a minute for DNS
az sql failover-group create says the name already exists | Failover group names are global DNS names | Delete your old group, or use a new SUFFIX
earliestRestoreDate is empty | The first full backup of the new database is not finished | Wait; it usually appears within about 30 minutes of setup.sh
az sql db restore refuses the point in time | The time is before the earliest restore point, or a log backup is still pending | Check earliestRestoreDate; wait ten minutes and run the restore again
Login failed for user '<token-identified principal>' | You are signed in to Azure as a different account from the servers' Entra admin | az account show --query user.name; sign in as the account that ran setup.sh
cleanup.sh reports that it could not delete something | A replication link or a running operation blocked it | Wait five minutes and run bash cleanup.sh again

Stretch goals

- Put Surabaya's orders back. Cross-database queries are not available in Azure SQL Database, so generate the INSERT statements from the restored copy and run them on the primary:
  azsql "$MAIN_FQDN" sqldb-orders-restored -h-1 -W -Q "SET NOCOUNT ON; SELECT CONCAT('SET IDENTITY_INSERT dbo.Orders ON; INSERT INTO dbo.Orders (OrderId, CustomerId, OrderDate, StoreCode, TotalIdr, Status) VALUES (', OrderId, ', ', CustomerId, ', ''', CONVERT(varchar(19), OrderDate, 126), ''', ''', StoreCode, ''', ', TotalIdr, ', ''', Status, '''); SET IDENTITY_INSERT dbo.Orders OFF;') FROM dbo.Orders WHERE StoreCode = 'SBY-01';" > sby-orders.sql
  cat sby-orders.sql
  azsql "$FOG_RW" "$DB" -i sby-orders.sql && rm sby-orders.sql

- Fail back to the main server with another planned failover (--server "$SQL_MAIN" --resource-group "$RG"), then run EXPECTED_PRIMARY=main bash verify.sh.
- Row-level security: create a predicate function and a security policy so that support_agent sees only orders from JKT-01, and test it with EXECUTE AS USER.
- Watch the lag move: insert a few hundred rows in a loop through $FOG_RW and query sys.dm_geo_replication_link_status while it runs.
- Read the backup settings in the portal (sqldb-orders › Data management › Backups): retention policies, the available restore points, and where long-term retention would be configured.

Challenge brief

Build the following, any way you like (portal, CLI, Bicep). setup.sh may create the starting point (items 1–3):

1. Two resource groups, rg-lunch28-<suffix> in $LOCATION and rg-lunch28-dr-<suffix> in $SECONDARY_LOCATION, created with ensure_rg (tagged course=azure-fundamentals-lunches and lunch=28).
2. Two logical servers, sql-nusa-main-<suffix> and sql-nusa-dr-<suffix>, one in each group, both with Microsoft Entra-only authentication and a firewall rule that allows your current Cloud Shell IP address.
3. A database sqldb-orders on the main server with dbo.Customers and dbo.Orders (use orders-dr.sql).
4. Dynamic data masking on dbo.Customers.Email.
5. A failover group fog-nusa-<suffix> that contains sqldb-orders, with the customer-managed (Manual) failover policy.
6. A database sqldb-orders-restored on the main server, created by point-in-time restore from a moment before you deleted the SBY-01 orders.
7. A completed planned failover: sql-nusa-dr-<suffix> is the primary of the failover group.
8. Optional: server auditing on both servers to a Log Analytics workspace log-nusa.

Then run bash verify.sh. Stuck? Peek at solution.sh or switch to Guided mode.
